title: Coin Detectives
sub: Grades 3–4 · Real or Replica? · Coins as evidence
objective: Students will read an ancient coin as a piece of evidence. They will use the clues experts use to tell a genuine coin from a fake, put the coins of the New Testament in time order, and explain how a coin made by a real ruler, in a real year, helps show that the Gospel happened in real places among real people.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A coin made by a real ruler, in a real year, is a witness. It helps show that the Gospel happened in real places, among real people.

Why would a Roman governor put a ladle used in pagan worship on a coin for Jewish people to spend?

steps.title: How do you know it’s real?
script: Hold up a modern coin. *“How do you know this coin is real and not a toy?”* Take answers: the weight, the shine, the words, where it came from. Then show the coin of Pontius Pilate on page 3. *“The man who put Jesus on trial had this coin made. An expert says it is real. Today you are the expert.”*

coin.label: Case 7 · Ministry and Passion
coin.title: The coin of Pontius Pilate
body: Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judaea from 26 to 36 AD. This coin was minted in 29 or 30 AD, within a few years of the Passion, which most scholars date to AD 30 or 33. One side shows a simpulum, a Roman ladle used in pagan worship; the other shows three ears of grain tied together. For decades some scholars questioned whether Pilate was real. In 1961 a stone carved with his name and title was found at Caesarea Maritima. This coin existed before that discovery. It was evidence all along.

steps.title: Struck by hand
script: **How ancient coins were made.** A blank of metal was struck between two engraved dies, by hand, one at a time. Striking leaves crisp, sharp detail — and everyday coins were often struck crude and off-center.

steps.title: Real or fake?
script: **How fakes are made.** Some are *cast*: molten metal is poured into a mold made from a real coin, which leaves soft detail, tiny bubbles or a grainy surface. Some are struck from *false dies*, copied by hand. Some are given fake age with a tumbler or sandpaper, or a patina painted on chemically. Play the widow’s mite round of *Real or Replica?* together and read its clue aloud: *“If a lepton looks perfect, be suspicious. The imperfection is the proof of authenticity.”*

steps.title: The proof
script: **The answer:** **Coin B.** A real lepton is crude, off-center and irregular; the fake is too clean and symmetrical, its patina applied by chemicals.

steps.title: Witnesses
script: **Why it matters.** Read Luke 3:1 aloud: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist’s preaching by naming Tiberius, Pontius Pilate and Herod, tetrarch of Galilee. The exhibition holds coins of all three: Pilate’s is genuine, and the coins of Tiberius and Herod Antipas are museum-quality replicas. A genuine coin is a witness from the same years as the Gospel.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels compare real and fake coins and put coins of the Gospel in order.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Spot the difference between a real and a fake widow’s mite using a checklist of clues. Read Pilate’s coin as evidence. Number four coins in story order, with pictures and dates.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Find the fake in two pairs and explain the clues in a table. Tell struck from cast. Order five coins by date, then explain why Pilate’s coin is evidence for the Gospel.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Weigh strong and weak evidence on the hardest kind of fake. Explain why it matters that three exhibition coins are replicas. Order five coins and explain the one that breaks the pattern.

steps.purpose: Practice the detective’s skills independently, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three compare real and fake coins, and put coins of the Gospel in order.

steps.title: A human timeline
script: Give five students the coins on page 3: Augustus, the Widow’s Mite, Pilate, Agrippa and Festus. The class arranges them in Gospel order, from the census at Jesus’ birth to Paul’s appeal to Caesar.
**Gospel order:** Augustus Caesar, Widow’s Mite, Pontius Pilate, Herod Agrippa I, Porcius Festus.
